title: The Liquor-Seller
summary: A single liquor-seller brews in two houses, binding her liquor with fine bark, and the refrain says it makes one ageless and deathless. A customer who sees a sign at the tenth door comes to her sixty-four pots and, once inside, does not come out; Virūpa ends with one narrow-spouted pot: make it steady and move it. Munidatta reads the liquor-seller and the pot as the avadhūtī (the central channel), the liquor as bodhicitta and the customer as the gandharva being entering by the door of Vairocana; his comment on couplet 4 survives only in the Tibetan translation.

flags.note: Shastri's heading line names only the rāga. The poet's name is supplied, in the brief's heading form, from the attribution virubāpādānāṃ, ‘of Virubāpāda’, written before the song (set aside from line 1a), and agrees with the Tibetan heading bi rU pa'i zhabs kyi'o, ‘of Virūpa’. The Tibetan names the melody chen po, ‘Great’, not Gavaṛā. Drop the name if headings should carry only what the heading line says.

lines.translit: eka se śuṇḍini dui ghare sāndhaa
lines.gloss: one · that, she · liquor-seller (f.) · two · in house(s) · brews / enters / joins (3sg)

flags.note: sāndhaa: (1) ‘brews, prepares’ (compare Sanskrit sandhāna, used of preparing liquor), chosen because the refrain gives the same verb the object bāruṇī, ‘liquor’, and because the Tibetan has chang spyod byed, ‘deals in beer’; (2) ‘enters’ (compare modern Bengali sẽdh-), giving ‘one liquor-seller enters two houses’; (3) ‘joins’, the sense of Munidatta's paraphrase sandhayati, to which he adds praveśayati, ‘makes enter’ (cp.03.m2).
eka se: ‘that one’; se may be the demonstrative or the pronoun ‘she’. Rendered simply ‘One’; the one-in-two riddle is kept.

lines.gloss: fine, smooth · with bark · liquor · binds (3sg) · refrain cue (not translated)

flags.note: bāndhaa: literally ‘binds, ties’; in brewing it may mean ‘sets, fixes’. ‘Binds’ is kept because it is the literal sense and Munidatta's gloss turns on it (bandhayati, cp.03.m2). The Tibetan has sbyor bar byed, ‘prepares, mixes’.

cīaṇa is taken as Sanskrit cikkaṇa, ‘smooth, fine’. The Tibetan reads phabs dang rtsi med, roughly ‘yeast and, without sap(?)’: phabs seems to render the bark as a starter, but rtsi med does not obviously answer to cīaṇa, and its sense is unclear.

lines.gloss: in the innate (or: the innate, as object) · steady · having made · liquor · brews (3sg; or imperative)
lines.en: She makes it [steady]{sthira} in the [innate]{sahaja} and brews the [liquor]{varuni},

flags.note: Two choices. (a) sahaje is read as locative, ‘in the innate’, with the object of ‘make steady’ unstated; Munidatta (sahajānandaṃ sthirīkṛtya, cp.03.m3) and the Tibetan (lhan cig skyes pa brtan par bzung) both make the innate itself what is made steady. (b) sāndhe is read as third person, ‘she brews’, continuing couplet 1 and matching hoi, ‘becomes’, in 2b; Munidatta reads the refrain as instruction to a novice yogi (bho bālayogin … tat kuru), which would give ‘Make it steady in the innate and brew the liquor’.

The Tibetan quotes the line as lhan cig skyes pa brtan par bzung kyi rnal 'byor chang: it has a vocative, ‘yogi’ (kyi is probably kye, ‘O’, as in the commentary's lemma kye rnal 'byor pa chang, cp.03.m3), and no verb answering to sāndhe.

lines.translit: jem̐ ajarāmara hoi diṭa kāndha(ndhaḥ) || dhru ||
lines.gloss: by which · ageless and deathless · becomes · firm · shoulder (trunk, body) · refrain cue (not translated)
lines.en: by which one becomes [ageless and deathless]{ajaramara}, firm-shouldered.

flags.note: kāndha is literally ‘shoulder’ (modern Bengali kā̃dh; Sanskrit skandha, also ‘trunk’ and, in Buddhist usage, ‘aggregate’). Chosen: ‘firm-shouldered’, describing the drinker. Alternatives: ‘firm in body’; or diṭa kāndha as subject, ‘by which the body becomes ageless, deathless and firm’, as the Tibetan takes it (phung po 'gyur med brtan, ‘the aggregates unchanging and firm’). Munidatta has dṛḍhaskandha, ‘a firm skandha’ (cp.03.m3).
Shastri prints kāndha(ndhaḥ), recording the variant kāndhaḥ; the sense is unaffected.

lines.gloss: tenth · at the door · sign · seeing (or: having shown)

flags.note: dekhaiā is read as ‘seeing, having seen’, with the customer of 3b as subject, as Munidatta (dṛṣṭvā, cp.03.m4) and the Tibetan (mthong bar 'gyur, ‘comes to be seen’) take it. The -ai- may instead mark a causative, ‘having shown’: the liquor-seller puts out a sign and the customer comes.

lines.gloss: came · customer · by himself · carrying, going · refrain cue (not translated)
lines.en: a [customer]{garahaka} came, making his own way.

flags.note: apaṇe bahiā: apaṇe is ‘by himself’; bahiā is a participle of vah-, ‘carry, bear, flow, travel’. ‘Making his own way’ tries to keep both. Alternatives: ‘of his own accord’ (Munidatta's svayam eva āgata, cp.03.m4, which does not gloss bahiā); ‘carrying it himself’ (the Tibetan: rang gis chang ni khur nas 'ongs, ‘came carrying beer himself’).

lines.gloss: sixty-four · in pots · sets out, gives · wares (stall)
lines.en: She sets out her [wares]{pasara} in sixty-four [pots]{pot};

flags.note: ghaṛi is ‘pot, water jar’ but also a period of about twenty-four minutes; the Tibetan gives both (chu tshod drug cu rtsa bzhi'i g+ha TA'i stegs bu, ‘a stall of ghaṭā of sixty-four hours’). pasārā may be the wares or the stall that shows them (Tibetan stegs bu, ‘platform, stall’). deṭa is taken as ‘gives, sets out’; the form is unusual.

lines.gloss: entered · customer · not · going out (exit) · refrain cue (not translated)
lines.en: the [customer]{garahaka} who has gone in does not come out.

flags.note: nisārā may be a noun, ‘exit’ (Sanskrit niḥsāra), giving ‘for the customer who has gone in there is no way out’; the sense is the same.
Munidatta's lemma reads eka gha ḍulī where the song has eka sa ḍulī, and he goes on to explain ghaṭī, ‘pot’ (cp.03.m5). The sense ‘one pot’ stands either way.
nāla is a tube, pipe or hollow stalk; ‘spout’ suits a pot. sarui may carry an emphatic -i (‘very narrow’); the Tibetan has shin tu phra, ‘very thin’.

lines.translit: bhaṇanti biruā thira kari cāla || dhru ||
lines.gloss: says (honorific pl.) · Biruā (Virūpa) · steady · having made · move (imperative) · refrain cue (not translated)
lines.en: [Virūpa]{p-virupa} says: make it [steady]{sthira} and move it.

flags.note: cāla: ‘move, set going’, supported by Munidatta's cālaya (cp.03.m5) and the Tibetan bskyod par gyis, ‘make it move’. With a narrow-spouted pot it might mean ‘tip’ or ‘pour’. The object is not stated.
The poet names himself Biruā; the glossary's Virūpa is used, as Lui becomes Lūyī elsewhere.

notes.text: A [rāga]{raga} is a melodic mode of Indian music; the heading names the one the song is sung to.

Shastri's heading line gives only the rāga. The poet's name comes from the attribution virubāpādānāṃ, ‘of Virubāpāda’, written before the song (Shastri prints it at the head of line 1a, where it has been set aside), and agrees with the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293), whose heading ends bi rU pa'i zhabs kyi'o, ‘of Virūpa’. Munidatta calls him Viruāpāda (cp.03.m1); the song calls him Biruā (5b). The Tibetan names the melody chen po zhes bya ba'i glu'i gdangs, ‘the melody called Great’, instead of Gavaṛā; perhaps the translators heard the vernacular baṛa, ‘big’, in gabaṛā, but that is only a guess.

Munidatta introduces the song as Viruāpāda's teaching, spoken with a mind moved again and again by supreme compassion, to make ‘that avadhūtikā’ plain beyond doubt by the distinction of the purified (pariśuddhabhedena). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has ‘by the division into purified and unpurified’ (yongs su dag pa dang yongs su ma dag pa'i dbye bas).

sāndhaa here and sāndhe in the refrain (2a) come from sāndh-, which can mean ‘enter’ (compare modern Bengali sẽdh-, ‘creep in’), ‘join’ (Sanskrit sandhā-), or ‘prepare’ liquor (compare Sanskrit sandhāna, used of fermenting and distilling). The draft reads ‘brews’ in both lines because in the refrain the verb takes bāruṇī, ‘liquor’, as its object. On the reading ‘enters’, 1a would say that one liquor-seller enters two houses. Munidatta paraphrases with sandhayati, ‘joins’, and adds praveśayati, ‘makes enter’ (cp.03.m2). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has chang ma gcig nyid khyim ni gnyis na chang spyod byed, ‘the one beer-woman deals in beer in two houses’, supplying ‘beer’.

The couplet is a scene of liquor-making. The liquor-seller (śuṇḍinī) follows a trade that caste society ranked low; her bāruṇī (Sanskrit vāruṇī) is a strong liquor, and bark may have served as a fermenting starter. ‘One woman in two houses’ is a riddle, and the draft keeps it as one.

Munidatta reads the liquor-seller as the [avadhūtī]{avadhuti}, the central channel of the subtle body: ‘she, the avadhūtikā, is the liquor-seller’. In his gloss the mature yogi joins the two powerful ones, the moon and the sun, left and right, at the opening of the bell in the ‘upper nose’, and makes them enter the middle channel (madhyamā); by this he makes self-blessing firm. Then, at the ‘lower nose’, the opening at the tip of the vajra jewel, he binds the drop of [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta} (the ‘mind of awakening’, here a bodily essence), called vāruṇī ‘because of the delight of bliss’. The ‘two’ are the moon and the sun; he does not repeat the word ‘house’. His opening words, ekakā ṣaṭpathayogāt (perhaps ‘single, through joining the six paths’), are obscure, and the syntax of the gloss is loose.

cīaṇa is probably Sanskrit cikkaṇa, ‘smooth, fine’ (compare Bengali cikan, ‘fine, thin’); bākala is bark (Sanskrit valkala). bāndhaa is ‘binds, ties’, perhaps here a brewer's word, ‘sets, fixes’; ‘binds’ keeps the literal sense, which Munidatta's gloss uses (bandhayati, cp.03.m2).

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads phabs dang rtsi med chu bdag chang ni sbyor bar byed, roughly ‘with yeast and, without sap(?), she prepares Varuṇa-beer’. It seems to take the bark as a starter (phabs, ‘yeast’); rtsi med does not obviously answer to cīaṇa. Shastri prints the refrain cue ধ্রু after this line too, before the refrain itself; it is not translated.

Munidatta calls this couplet the refrain ([dhruvapada]{dhruvapada}) and says that with it the poet makes ultimate bodhicitta firm. He takes it as instruction to a novice yogi (bho bālayogin): by the grace of the vajra guru, make innate joy steady through the joy of cessation; understand vāruṇī, a twilight word, as conventional bodhicitta; bind that bodhicitta, gone to self-blessing, with the noose of imperishable bliss, and do the special practice by which you gain agelessness and deathlessness and a firm skandha (dṛḍhaskandha). He adds a verse from the Yogaratnamālā calling emptiness the vajra. The song's own verbs need not be second person; see the flag on 2a.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) quotes the line as lhan cig skyes pa brtan par bzung kyi rnal 'byor chang, ‘holding the innate steady, O yogi, beer’. Like Munidatta it makes the innate what is held steady; it has a vocative, rnal 'byor, ‘yogi’ (kyi is probably kye, ‘O’, as in the commentary's lemma kye rnal 'byor pa chang), and no verb answering to sāndhe. The vocative may come from Munidatta's bho bālayogin (cp.03.m3) rather than from a different Bengali reading.

kāndha is literally ‘shoulder’ (modern Bengali kā̃dh), from Sanskrit skandha, which also means ‘trunk’ and, in Buddhist usage, the aggregates. diṭa (Sanskrit dṛḍha) is ‘firm’. diṭa kāndha may describe the drinker, ‘firm-shouldered’, or be the subject, ‘by which the trunk becomes ageless, deathless and firm’. Munidatta has dṛḍhaskandha, a firm skandha gained with agelessness (cp.03.m3); the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads gang gis rgas dang 'chi med phung po 'gyur med brtan, ‘by which the aggregates are ageless, deathless, unchanging and firm’, taking skandha as the aggregates.
Freedom from old age and death (ajarāmara) is what the elixirs of Indian alchemy and the siddhas' bodily yoga promised; in the song it is what the liquor gives.

dekhaiā is read as ‘seeing’, with the customer of 3b as the one who sees, as Munidatta (dṛṣṭvā, ‘having seen’, cp.03.m4) and the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293: sgo ni bcu par rtags kyis mtshon pa mthong bar 'gyur, ‘at the tenth door what is marked by a sign comes to be seen’) take it. The -ai- may instead mark a causative, ‘having shown’: the liquor-seller puts out a sign and the customer comes.

The sign (cihna) may be a shop sign: Sanskrit calls a vintner dhvajin, ‘one with a flag’, which suggests that liquor shops advertised themselves. ‘The tenth door’ is literal in the line; yogic literature counts nine openings of the body and adds a hidden tenth, which the phrase may evoke.

Munidatta, ‘with the next verse’ (padāntareṇa, his second), reads the tenth door as the door of [Vairocana]{p-vairocana} and the customer as the [gandharva]{gandharva} being (in Buddhist doctrine, the being between death and rebirth that enters the womb): seeing at that door the sign of the delight of the bliss of [great passion]{maharaga}, it comes of itself, enters by that door, and takes its pleasure by drinking the juice of the lotus of great bliss. He quotes a verse of Kāṇha: taking [evaṃkāra]{evamkara} (the syllables e and vaṃ) as its seed, the lotus has blossomed; the hero of pleasure, in the form of a bee, smells its nectar; Kāṇha says the mind is not broken at all; the motionless wind stays in the housewife's house.

The Tibetan translation of Munidatta's comment (Toh 2293) ends with a question and answer that the Sanskrit lacks: ‘How does one meditate by oneself?’, answered from the Hevajra: ‘oneself the maker, oneself the destroyer, oneself the king, oneself the lord’.

apaṇe is ‘by himself’ (Sanskrit ātman-); bahiā is a participle of vah-, ‘carry, bear, flow, travel’. Munidatta's svayam eva āgata, ‘came of himself’ (cp.03.m4), answers to apaṇe and does not gloss bahiā. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads chang nyo 'ongs pa rang gis chang ni khur nas 'ongs, ‘the beer-buyer who came came carrying beer himself’, taking bahiā as ‘carrying’ and supplying ‘beer’. garāhaka is Sanskrit grāhaka, ‘buyer’, a word that in Buddhist philosophy also means ‘grasper’, the perceiving subject; Munidatta does not use that sense here.

ghaṛi is a pot or water jar (Sanskrit ghaṭī, ghaṭikā); the same word names a period of about twenty-four minutes, measured with a water clock. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) gives both: chu tshod drug cu rtsa bzhi'i g+ha TA'i stegs bu bshams, ‘she set out a stall of ghaṭā of sixty-four hours’, where chu tshod, ‘water-time’, is the Tibetan word for that period and g+ha TA transcribes the Indic word. pasārā is goods spread out for sale, or the stall that shows them (Sanskrit prasāra); the Tibetan has stegs bu, ‘platform, stall’. deṭa is taken as ‘gives, sets out’, from de-, ‘give’; the form is unusual.

Munidatta's comment on this couplet survives only in the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293); the Nepal manuscript has no comment on couplet 4. There he says that with the third verse the poet speaks of the stopping of the gandharva being's going, that is, its passage to rebirth. He takes the sixty-four as the sixty-four lotus petals and ghaṭī as twilight language for the [wheel of emanation]{nirmana-cakra}, and says the stall (stegs bu), also twilight language, is the seat; into it the gandharva being enters from the blazing fire of great passion, and its entry has no coming out. He quotes Kāṇha: free of the two entries, below and above, it stays there unmoving; Kāṇha says the mind goes nowhere and is not cut off; with the motionless wind it circles in the housewife's house. The Tibetan syntax is loose, and the Sanskrit behind it is lost.

paiṭhela is ‘entered’ (Sanskrit praviṣṭa); nisārā is ‘going out, exit’ (Sanskrit niḥsāra). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) calls the customer here chang 'thung, ‘beer-drinker’ (in 3b chang nyo, ‘beer-buyer’), and reads rab tu zhugs nas nges par byung ba med, ‘having fully entered, there is no coming out’. Munidatta's comment, which survives only in the Tibetan, echoes the line: the gandharva being's entry has no coming out (cp.03.m6).

Munidatta's lemma reads eka gha ḍulī where the song has eka sa ḍulī, and he goes on to explain ghaṭī, ‘pot’ (cp.03.m5); his manuscript may have had gha, perhaps short for ghaṛi or ghaṭī, in place of sa, ‘that’. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads chang gi bum pa gcig gi mchu ni shin tu phra, ‘the spout of one beer pot is very thin’, supplying ‘beer’; its shin tu, ‘very’, may render an emphatic -i in sarui.

Munidatta takes the one pot as the avadhūtikā he spoke of before: it is called ghaṭī because it joins (ghaṭati) the two truths, conventional and ultimate, and it is subtle in form because it stops the two appearances, which he seems to match with the narrow spout. Through that channel of semen (śukranāḍikā), by the guru's instruction, the yogi is to make the unfallen bodhicitta steady and move it in a waveless way; so he reads thira kari cāla. He adds a verse from the Sekoddeśa on the luminous stream of the moon that must not fall.

Where the Sanskrit introduces this couplet as ‘the fourth instruction’ (caturthopadeśa), the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has rkang pa bzhi pa, ‘the fourth verse’, which fits Munidatta's count of verses without the refrain. The Tibetan's sna gnyis 'gog pa, ‘stopping the two nostrils’, stands where the Sanskrit has ābhāsadvayanirodha, ‘stopping the two appearances’, and may be a slip for snang gnyis, ‘the two appearances’.

bhaṇanti is an honorific plural, ‘says’. The poet names himself Biruā, the vernacular form of Virūpa. thira kari cāla is ‘making it steady, move it’; cāl- is ‘move, set going’, and with a narrow-spouted pot it could mean ‘tip’ or ‘pour’, but ‘move’ is kept, as Munidatta's cālaya (cp.03.m5) and the Tibetan translation's brtan pa nyid du bskyod par gyis, ‘make it move in steadiness’, both support. The object is not stated.

proposals.definition: A sign or mark (Sanskrit cihna). In song 3 a sign is seen at the tenth door and a customer comes, perhaps like the sign that advertised a liquor shop. Munidatta speaks of the sign of the delight of the bliss of great passion seen at the door of Vairocana (cp.03.m4). The Tibetan translation has rtags.
proposals.symbolicImage: a sign seen at the tenth door

symbolicReadings.referent: the sign of the delight of the bliss of great passion (mahārāgasukhapramodacihna), which the gandharva being sees at the door of Vairocana before it enters

proposals.rationale: cihna recurs in the songs and in Munidatta (the sign here; the mark of the lord of yogis and the yoginī's own mark in song 4). One entry keeps ‘sign’ consistent and keeps the literal sign apart from Munidatta's reading.

proposals.definition: Steady, still (Old Bengali thira, Sanskrit sthira): in the siddhas' songs, often the steadiness a yogi gives to mind, breath or vital essence so that it neither wavers nor falls. In song 3 the refrain and the last couplet both speak of making something steady; Munidatta names innate joy (cp.03.m3) and the unfallen bodhicitta (cp.03.m5).
proposals.symbolicImage: making something steady (the object is unstated in the song)

symbolicReadings.referent: innate joy, made steady through the joy of cessation by the grace of the vajra guru
the unfallen bodhicitta, made steady through the channel of semen and moved without waves

proposals.rationale: thira recurs in the songs as a word of yogic practice, twice in this song (refrain and bhaṇitā). Fixing ‘steady’ keeps it distinct from diṭa, ‘firm’ (Sanskrit dṛḍha), and records where Munidatta supplies the unstated object. The Tibetan brtan renders both thira and diṭa, so it is not used for matching.

questions: Refrain (2a–2b): I read sāndhe as third person, ‘she brews’, continuing couplet 1 and matching hoi, ‘becomes’. Munidatta reads the refrain as instruction to a novice yogi, which would give ‘Make it steady in the innate and brew the liquor’. Which do you want?
sāndh- (1a, 2a): ‘brews’ is my choice; ‘enters’ (compare modern Bengali sẽdh-) would make 1a ‘One liquor-seller enters two houses’. Please confirm, or choose ‘enters’ for 1a only.
kāndha (2b): I kept the literal ‘firm-shouldered’. Would you rather have ‘firm in body’, or the Tibetan's syntax, ‘by which the body becomes ageless, deathless and firm’?

Heading: should it name the poet, whose name comes from the attribution before the song and not from Shastri's heading line? And should the name be the glossary's ‘Virūpa’ or ‘Virūpāda’, like the brief's example ‘Lūyīpāda’? In the bhaṇitā I used ‘Virūpa’ for the song's Biruā.
apaṇe bahiā (3b): is ‘making his own way’ acceptable, or do you prefer ‘of his own accord’ (closer to Munidatta) or ‘carrying it himself’ (closer to the Tibetan)?
dekhaiā (3a): I read ‘seeing’ with Munidatta and the Tibetan. Do you want the causative, ‘She puts out a sign at the tenth door’, considered instead?
Proposals: are cihna (‘sign’) and sthira (‘steady’) worth glossary entries? I marked both in the lines; if you reject them, the markup in 2a, 3a and 5b should be removed.
